newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RUGBY LEAGUE-SUPER LEAGUE CHASES RIVAL PLAYERS.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY LEAGUE-SUPER LEAGUE CHASES RIVAL PLAYERS.

text.p: Media baron Rupert Murdoch's Super League said on Tuesday it planned to recruit top players from clubs loyal to Australia's established rugby league body.
Super League chief executive John Ribot said his organisation intended to open negotiations with players under contract with the Australian Rugby League (ARL), the sport's traditional rulers.
The move follows Super League's comprehensive legal victory over the ARL on Friday when an appeals court reversed an earlier ban and freed Murdoch's rebel competition to kick off next year.
"Super League believes that all players should have the freedom to chose which competition they wish to compete in," Ribot said in a statement.

The ARL responded by declaring that its contracts with its players were still valid and announced a multi-million dollar funding deal with its major financial backer, pay television operator Optus Vision.

"It (the funding) will ensure that the ARL's loyal clubs and players have the backing to survive News Ltd's attempts to take over rugby league," the ARL said, referring to Murdoch's Australian media subsidiary.
The announcement increases the likelihood of Super League and the ARL running rival competitions in Australia next year.

Earlier, Ribot said Super League lawyers believe the players will be free to switch camps because their current ARL contracts amounted to an "unreasonable restraint of trade" and were therefore invalid.
Ribot said the agreements appeared designed to prevent players from choosing their employers for up to 10 years after the contract expires without the support of any guaranteed employment.

The breakaway Super League, backed by News Ltd, has recovered the initiative after being forced to scrap its planned launch in March because of an earlier court order barring it from starting in Australia before 2000.
The Federal Court originally ruled that all existing clubs, including eight teams loyal to Super League, had to honour agreements binding them to the ARL until then.
But rebel clubs were released from that commitment on Friday when the court upheld News Ltd's appeal and ruled that the loyalty pacts were invalid.
